via Sacramento Bee

Major meeting in Sioux Falls Tuesday on proposed hyperscale data center

2026-10-24, updated: 2026-10-25

Editor’s note: You can observe the proceedings of the meeting and have an opportunity to speak. It’s set to discuss a proposed data center between Brandon and Sioux Falls on Tuesday, October 27, 7pm, Carnegie Town Hall, 235 W. 10th St. in Sioux Falls.

The issue of data centers has become a hot button, with the right and the left finding common ground. Democrats, Republicans, Independents and all others have coalesced around opposition to having them anywhere near our own communities.

And for good reasons: they suck the local energy sector dry, which will cause our electricity to fluctuate and cost us dearly in our pocketbooks … they do the same with the local water supply, and it’s unclear how much damage to water tables and our private supplies they will cause … they create noise at decibels well above the safety level for human well-being, and that also includes all the nearby wildlife and insects as well … and the profligate amount of diesel fuel they will house threatens our air and the environment with constant and unabated spills and leaks into the Earth.

On October 27, the Sioux Falls Council and the Lincoln County Commissioners will meet jointly to address the issue of data centers, particularly the Gemini Data Center, which is a proposed hyperscale data center on 164 acres between Brandon and Sioux Falls. There were hours of opposition remarks and testimony given to the SF Council this past January, yet the immediate vote in favor of the 500 megawatt Gemini project was 7-0.

Yet now the politicians have realized this has turned into a real issue with huge public opposition, so they’ve established an Oversight Committee to study potential future regulations on data centers and to gather more public input. This is what the October 27 meeting is all about and I suggest you, dear reader, make every effort to be there.

At least one of the public needs to suggest to the politicians that mitigation is the answer for all of us.

  1. on the power issue, any data center should have its own wind turbine (or more) and a solar roof and solar farm. These will not suffice on their own but will help mitigate the huge power needs of each data center.

  2. on the water issue, a closed loop system should always be employed and all the water used is to be recycled, so as little as possible is taken from the local supply.

  3. on the sound pollution issue, a 30-foot fence should be built around the entire data center itself. Such fences have proven to substantially mitigate the sound from interstate highways, so this fence (to include a closed gate) would help mitigate the noise.

  4. hundreds of diesel generators are expected for power augmentation purposes. Emission control devices can mitigate the air pollution of these generators, and fuel containment should be treated as part of critical infrastructure planning (for any and all future leaks).

There are many more issues concerning data centers, but these four stand out as the biggest and most critical. These politicians live here, too, and if they do not require these things, do you really think any company would voluntarily pay these expenses? Besides insisting that our local politicians pass regulations such as mentioned here, they should also eschew any thoughts of tax breaks.

The companies behind these centers represent billions of dollars and they fully intend to make a financial killing on these centers.

We cannot stop them, but we can regulate them and force them to mitigate the coming harm to our communities.

Van Carter of Sioux Falls is a retired broadcast journalist and environmentalist who published a green website for 15 years.

via Electrek Feed

Media concentration. It's happening nationally and locally

2026-10-23, updated: 2026-10-25

The assertion that a strong democracy needs strong newspapers has been a popular cliche for generations. We might want to take the cliche seriously at a time when both our democracy and our independent news media appear to be in jeopardy.

Increasingly, independent newspapers are going out of business or being purchased by oligarchs and TV networks are consolidating into fewer and fewer hands. About 40% of America's newspapers have shut down since the year 2000. With support from the Trump administration, Paramount Skydance purchased Warner Brothers, including CNN, creating an enormous media empire. David Ellison of Skydance installed Bari Weiss, a right-wing influencer, at CBS News, where she has sought to control the content of news stories while many veteran journalists have resigned. Recently, Weiss has insisted that CBS News pursue negative stories on two Democratic U.S. Senate candidates who are running in highly competitive races: Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas. The recent allegation that Talarico had checked into a mental health facility in Ohio proved to be utterly false.

Jeff Bezos, the founder and Chair of Amazon, now owns the Washington Post, which has been one of America's most esteemed newspapers for more than a century. Interestingly, the Post cost Bezos less than half of what he paid for his new super yacht. Bezos has steered the newspaper away from its perceived liberal bias, not wanting to irritate President Trump.

Across the country, investigative journalism is in trouble, and media organizations concentrate their energies, and their dwindling field reporters, on "feel good" human interest stories. When late night TV personalities like Jimmy Kimmel and Stephen Colbert chose to interview Talarico, those interviews were not allowed to air on their programs. Interestingly enough, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) abandoned the Fairness Doctrine, which required equal time for both sides of a political controversy, back in 1987. That does not affect the desire of media titans to avoid rocking the boat by giving exposure to politicians they do not like.

Here in South Dakota, the decline of independent media is obvious. Weekly newspapers in rural communities continue to shut their doors. Lee Enterprises, which owns the Rapid City Journal, had been saddled with debt ever since it purchased the Pulitzer newspaper chain at a time when readership was about to decline sharply. The Journal now comes out just three times a week, and it no longer covers state and local government as diligently as it did in the past. The staff of reporters is stretched mighty thin.

The masthead of the Rapid City Journal now includes a daily reminder that David Hoffmann of the Hoffmann Media Group is now the "majority shareholder" of the corporation. Interestingly, Lee Enterprises recently purchased the Sioux Falls Argus Leader, the Watertown Public Opinion and the Aberdeen American News, giving it a virtual monopoly of major papers in South Dakota similar to the monopoly that it enjoys in Montana. In South Dakota and nationally, there is a diminished news media in fewer hands. Fewer and fewer reporters are watching, and reporting on, our public policy makers. We can continue to hope that our democracy survives.

Jay Davis is a retired Rapid City attorney

via Market Place Tech Report

Moderate Republicans and Democrats have a decision to make

2026-10-22, updated: 2026-10-25

Moderate Republicans and Democrats have a decision to make. Are they going to stick with their now weak party labels or are they going to break ranks?

The U.S. Senate race includes the incumbent, Senator Mike Rounds. His votes have supported the numerous cutbacks in funding which have negatively affected all of us in one way or another. His silence on numerous important issues is beyond concerning. He wants another term.

The Democrats had a candidate who decided to step aside. Lots of reasons and some back stories to that decision.

Then there is the independent Brian Bengs. He has a solid military career. Was a JAG lawyer. He has been a college professor. He is assertive without being obnoxious. He is listening to us. He wants to take what he is hearing and be OUR voice in the Senate.

Here is the math: Democrats have about 130,000 members. Republicans have a little over 300,000. Independents and no party affiliation voters are about 150,000. 20,000 more than Democrats, and about half as many as Republicans.

Most people I listen to want change in Washington. They are tired of the daily/hourly drama. Their ability to pay bills is harder now because of continuing inflation. They are not happy about tariffs and cuts in programs which help us.

If we truly want change in Washington, Democrats will have to vote in large numbers for Bengs. Same for Independents. An important component is Republicans, many of whom are not happy with Rounds, will have to cross the forbidden line.

Pols done by reputable firms show Bengs either slightly ahead or within the “margin of error.”   It is possible an Independent can win this year.

In Nebraska and Idaho, the Independents running for U.S. Senate are both within the “margin of error.”

If Bengs and the other two can win, there will be five Independents in the U.S. Senate. Enough numbers that both parties will have to pay attention to them.

Voting really matters now. More than ever. Remember in the race for Mayor of Sioux Falls this summer, only FOUR votes separated the top two candidates.

I am optimistic that positive change is coming to Washington. It would be wonderful if South Dakota, you and I are part it.

So, to my diehard Democrat friends, hold your nose if you must and vote for change. To my Republican friends, we are in this mess because of leaders in what used to be a proud, honest, compassionate party. You may need to hold your nose too, and vote for change.

Rick Knobe is a former mayor of Sioux Falls and long time radio talk show host, now retired

via Sacramento Bee

‘Anti-socialist’ Trump announces an $8 billion bailout for farmers.

2026-10-21, updated: 2026-10-25

Scrambling for votes at a Kansas Republican pep party last night, President Trump pledged that USDA will be making $8 billion in direct cash payments to American farmers. Combined with the $40 billion he’s already shelled out over the course of his two terms, Trump has given $48 billion in cash to farmers.

Much as I support cash assistance to American farmers – a stable ag economy is probably the  cornerstone of food and national security – this business of Trump financially harming our country’s ag sector with his counter-productive tariffs and inflation-driving foreign policies is getting old and expensive.

As to yesterday’s announcement, farmers shouldn’t be overly enthused about it. Scott Lincicome, VP of General Economics at the Cato Institute calls it “a band-aid on a flesh wound,” adding that at four thousand dollars a farm, “it might cover a few weeks of diesel costs.” As with other announcements (specifically, Russian diesel and imported ground beef) in recent months, Trump is fond of throwing out headline numbers that sound impressive but in actuality don’t do much in the way of helping farmers out with their double economic whammy of low crop prices and high input costs.

More generally, Trump’s reflexive need to look like he’s doing something substantive for producers and consumers has the unexpected political consequence of defining him as that word that he abhors — a socialist.

Disagree? If you consider socialism to be a system where the government intervenes in free market processes by altering free market outcomes, then Trump’s bailout is de facto socialism.

He has said “our country will never be a socialist country,” but, as with many of his other utterances, the president’s rhetoric often contradicts the president's reality.

Paying off farmers for financial troubles created by Trump’s flawed policies has been a recurring theme through both of his terms. He may hate the term, but when he needs to be, Trump is a socialist.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

via Sacramento Bee

The hidden costs of artificial intelligence: Are you paying attention?

2026-10-20, updated: 2026-10-25

According to an August 2026 article in Business Insider, a Microsoft employee ran up $28,000 in artificial intelligence charges in 28 days without buying anything.

He was using AI tools to do his job, and the company was billed for what the industry calls tokens. A token is a small unit of work: you ask one of these systems a question, it breaks the question into pieces and works through them, and each piece is a billable token.

AI tokens make up a new kind of business expense that companies are beginning to budget for. Individual users will eventually see this cost, too, even though most AI tools are still free or nearly free.

I recently encountered this myself when I hit a usage limit on an AI tool in the middle of a project. Not wanting to wait five hours for the allowance to reset, I told it to bill me for the overage. It only took 15 minutes to burn through nearly $50. Because I had notifications turned on, I could see the meter running and shut down the program.

Without that real-time notification, I might have gone merrily on my way until I finished my project, then been shocked when I realized what it had cost. This may well be what happened for the Microsoft employee who ran up the headline-worthy tab.

Tokens, like subscriptions and utility bills, are metered money. If I buy a five-dollar cup of coffee and swipe a card or hand over cash, I actively participate in the transaction. Metered money, by contrast, runs up in the background. We tend not to notice it because we are not deliberately deciding to spend it in the moment.

If you are among the many people beginning to use AI tools, be aware that at some point you will need to budget for them. Here are few ideas to help you avoid expensive surprises.

Be aware that paid AI services are likely to follow the same patterns as other metered services. A subscription model is a series of small yeses. This app or that service seems worth trying out for a small amount. Then, even if we don’t continue to use it, it keeps renewing until we notice that we’re paying for something we’ve forgotten to cancel. These systems are built so that paying takes no effort, which is exactly why the charges go unnoticed.

The pattern especially worth watching is the free tier that turns into a paid one. Metered services often start out free or at a low cost. The price then increases once you have built the habit of using the service.

Token billing will be even harder to plan for than subscriptions, because it is not a fixed or predictable monthly amount. It moves with how much the tool gets used, which makes it easy to underestimate.

If you are a fan of AI, how can you use it and also protect your budget? First, research any tools you might use so you understand the potential charges. Then set a number now for what these tools are worth to you in a month. Put any metered charges on one card, so you’ll have a monthly total you can see.

Budgeting in advance means making an active, deliberate decision. If you wait for the statement and react, you are passing judgment on yourself after the fact. This rarely changes what anyone does the next month.

For many people, AI tools will be worth paying for. However, it is wise to decide, before any bills arrive, how much in very real money those tools are worth to you.

What exactly is the just-launched Vote Independent Movement?

2026-10-19, updated: 2026-10-25

What exactly is the Vote Independent Movement?

I have been an independent my entire adult life.

Not because I believe Democrats and Republicans are the same. They aren’t. Not because I split my vote evenly between them. I don’t. And not because I think “independent” is another word for moderate.

Mostly, I’ve stayed independent because my beliefs have never fit neatly enough inside a political party to hand one my loyalty in advance.

That distinction has become unexpectedly relevant to my work.

This week, independent U.S. Senate candidate Brian Bengs launched the Vote Independent Movement, or VIM, a new project built around a two-sentence pledge: I pledge to consider every problem based on objective facts. I am not and will not be bound to automatically support the platform of, or the leaders of, any political party.

Brian founded it. I serve as its director.

So what exactly is it? For now, the simplest answer is the most accurate one: VIM is a movement built around a pledge, not a new political party.

That’s it.

There is no requirement to change your voter registration. A Republican can take it and remain a Republican. A Democrat can take it and remain a Democrat. An independent can take it without committing to vote for independent candidates.

And, importantly, taking the pledge does not commit someone to voting for Brian Bengs.

That last point is worth explaining because VIM’s origin is unusual.

Brian created the movement during his campaign for U.S. Senate, and VIM is currently a project of the Bengs campaign, paid for by the campaign.

Bengs says the idea grew out of his experience campaigning across South Dakota and repeatedly encountering people frustrated by the expectation that supporting a political party also requires automatically supporting its leaders and positions.

That experience led to a broader question: Is political independence primarily a voter-registration category, or can it describe a way of approaching politics?

The numbers make the question interesting.

Gallup reported in January that a record 45% of U.S. adults identified politically as independents in 2025, compared with 27% each identifying as Republicans and Democrats.

In South Dakota, 156,908 of 626,871 active registered voters are Independent or No Party Affiliation, more than the number registered as Democrats.

But those numbers have limits.

They don’t tell us why someone registered without a party. They don’t mean 45% of Americans share a political philosophy. And they certainly don’t mean those people agree with one another.

In some ways, that’s the more interesting part.

VIM isn’t attempting to create a platform that all those people agree on. The pledge doesn’t say what to believe about abortion, immigration, taxes, guns, health care, war or data centers. Two people could take it, examine the same issue honestly, and reach completely different conclusions.

The agreement is about the process: evidence first, conclusion second. Party label doesn’t settle the question.

The premise is that this matters most when the problems are hard. From the cost of living and rural health care to Social Security and trillion-dollar deficits, our country isn’t short on problems whose solutions demand serious choices. VIM’s argument is simply that party loyalty shouldn’t determine the answer before the facts do.

There is another question we deliberately haven’t answered yet: What does VIM become after Election Day?

We don’t know.

The website says so plainly. It could remain a movement, become an organization or take another form. The immediate experiment is much narrower: put the pledge in front of people, count how many take it, and see whether the idea has life beyond the campaign that produced it.

That uncertainty is real, not coyness.

I’ve spent much of the past year working in South Dakota politics and creating spaces where people with very different political beliefs can actually hear one another. One thing I’ve learned is that “independent” is an imprecise word. It can describe a registration, an ideology, a temperament, a protest against the two-party system or simply a person who doesn’t want a label.

VIM is testing another definition.

Independent can be a verb.

Look at the facts. Question your own side. Allow yourself to change your mind. Then decide.

Whether enough people find meaning in that definition to build something lasting around it is the part we don’t know yet.

And that’s probably the most interesting part of the experiment.

Ngoc Thach lives in South Dakota and is the director of the Vote Independent Movement

via Sacramento Bee

South Dakota farm loans need more than rising land values

2026-10-17, updated: 2026-10-25

Editor’s note: The author is a professor of Economics in Brazil. His research includes studies of American rural economics, including economic issues here in South Dakota.

Rising farmland values can give a farm room to borrow. Using that room to finance another season also gives the farm more debt to repay. South Dakota’s agricultural debate needs to keep both sides of that transaction in view, especially when the land market and the income earned from working the land move at different speeds.

SDSU Extension’s 2026 farm real estate survey estimates that average-productivity, nonirrigated cropland was worth $6,268 an acre statewide, up 1.3% from 2025. The average cash rental rate fell by $6, to $160 an acre. The reported gross rent-to-value ratio was 2.6%, before property taxes and other landlord expenses. That ratio describes rental income relative to land value. It does not measure a farm operator’s profit or ability to repay a loan.

These are regional survey estimates, with substantial variation across South Dakota, rather than appraisals of individual properties. Their significance is the different direction of land values and rents: the price of an asset can remain firm even as one source of income from it weakens. A stronger balance sheet deserves attention, but so does the money available to meet the next payment.

Recent credit evidence reinforces that distinction without justifying a blanket verdict on South Dakota farms. An August 2026 Kansas City Federal Reserve analysis of surveys across participating districts found that farm income and loan repayment conditions continued to weaken in the second quarter, although the deterioration eased. Agricultural land values remained supportive. Those regional findings should not be mistaken for a measure of distress on every South Dakota farm.

Land equity is valuable financial protection. It can support access to credit and give an owner flexibility during a difficult season. Yet borrowing against appreciation converts that flexibility into a future claim on income. The relevant question is whether the new debt buys time for an operation capable of recovering, or finances a shortfall that will return with the next production cycle.

The distinction is sharper for a tenant farmer. Appreciation belongs to the landowner, while rent is an expense for the operator. An owner farming partly rented acreage faces both positions at once. Treating rising land values as a general improvement in agriculture can therefore obscure how differently the same market affects the people producing on that land.

Lenders assessing the next advance need to distinguish recoverable collateral from cash available for repayment. A farm with valuable land may still need a different payment schedule; a borrower with little land may have an operation that generates reliable income. Public discussion of agricultural finance should leave room for those differences.

A practical starting point is a cash forecast that follows the production calendar far enough to capture the next season’s obligations. SDSU Extension recommends a rolling 18-month forecast, regularly compared with actual results. Annual totals can conceal a shortage between paying for inputs and receiving sales proceeds. Including household withdrawals and payments to equipment dealers or input suppliers makes the financing need easier to see.

That forecast should show what happens when a plausible setback arrives. A lower selling price may leave sufficient collateral but insufficient cash for scheduled payments. A delayed sale can create a timing problem even when the operation remains profitable. These problems call for different responses. The useful test is whether available cash and agreed credit can cover the weakest part of the season, with assumptions that the farmer and lender can explain.

Rescheduling a payment may solve a timing mismatch. Moving unpaid operating debt into a longer loan can also be reasonable when a credible recovery plan supports it. But extending the term cannot, by itself, make recurring losses sustainable. A larger pledge of land may protect a lender’s recovery while leaving the farm’s underlying financing problem unresolved.

This also matters when public support is assessed. A payment can relieve immediate pressure, but its success should be judged against the obligations it helps a farm meet and the borrowing that remains necessary afterward. Rising land prices alone cannot establish that an operation has recovered. Owners with substantial equity and producers with little owned land will need different financial judgments.

South Dakota has good reason to value the wealth held in its agricultural land. Preserving that wealth requires decisions grounded in the operation’s capacity to generate cash. Before more acreage secures another season’s borrowing, the repayment plan should explain how that season helps the farm carry its debt into the future.

Gustavo Pessoa is a professor of economics at Fundação Getulio Vargas in São Paulo, Brazil. His research focuses on financial stability, regulation and public policy.

New ‘lawyer’ shows Trump wants loyalty, not credibility

2026-10-16, updated: 2026-10-25

“Totalitarianism in power invariably replaces all first-rate talents, regardless of their sympathies, with those crackpots and fools whose lack of intelligence and creativity is still the best guarantee of their loyalty.” – Hannah Arendt, “The Origins of Totalitarianism” (1951)

In a breathtaking display of organizational indifference to the intelligence of the American public, the Trump administration this week trotted out a new press secretary who turned out to be a dud. She’s already gotten famous – and for all the wrong reasons – but in case you missed it, a few days ago Katie Zacharia took on the role of press secretary to the Trump administration.

Why is she a dud? It’s all about her credentials and the fact that she’s stretching the language about them. Lacking a license to practice, she says she’s a lawyer, but is she?

I don’t think so, but who am I? Let’s see what the arbiters of the English language have to say:

Per Merriam-Webster, a lawyer is “one whose profession is to conduct lawsuits for clients or to advise as to legal rights and obligations in other matters.”

The Oxford English Dictionary says a lawyer is “ a person who is trained and qualified to advise people about the law and to represent them in court, and to write legal documents.”

By those definitions, Zacharia is not a lawyer.

The news about her questionable claim is circulating widely, but not before some quickly bought it:

Bamboozled, Fox News described her (highlights mine) as “an attorney and television commentator.” Concurrently duped, President Trump on Truth Social said, “Katie is a distinguished Graduate of Pepperdine University, and the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, an attorney.”

Turns out, Zacharia has never passed a bar exam. Undeterred by reality, she has consistently claimed to be a lawyer. She has provided some tortured explanations about why she can call herself a lawyer even though she is not licensed to practice law, but her need to do so flies against commonly understood usage — and smacks of misrepresentation.

It’s amazing that nobody in the White House did a modicum of checking on this imposter before she was given the go-ahead to be the president’s spokesperson, but then, Zacharia is just the latest example of how the Trump administration has loaded itself up with people whose qualifications are questionable.

You can see why Hannah Arendt’s vivid depiction of how totalitarians pick their staffers, more on the basis of fealty than competence, quickly came to mind as I read this story.

So does that put Trump on the totalitarian track?

Much as it seems like that’s what he wants, he’ll come up way short. Trump’s awful handling of his office has driven his approval ratings to such lows that I doubt he’ll ever muster the kind of mass support that, as Hannah Arendt has argued, was necessary to bring post-19th century totalitarian regimes to power.

Trump’s team of incompetent sycophants has bungled its way into ruining his current term. These “crackpots and fools who lack intelligence and creativity,” Zacharia among them, will extend their hopeless track record until Trump and his people leave the White House.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

Should Climate Activists Keep Fighting Fossil Fuel Infrastructure?

2026-10-16

No researcher has been more cited in lawsuits against fossil fuel infrastructure than Peter Erickson. As an affiliated researcher at the Stockholm Environment Institute, Peter studies how pipelines and other oil and gas supply expansions can increase global carbon emissions. His work has been critical to the activist fights against the Keystone XL pipeline, the Enbridge pipeline, and others.

But in recent years, he’s taken a more nuanced approach to fossil fuel supply — in part because, as he has shown, it can enrich the oil and gas industry in a surprising but direct way. On this episode of Shift Key, Peter joins Rob to discuss why blocking fossil fuel supply can lower emissions, why it can counterintuitively transfer wealth from energy consumers to fossil fuel firms, and what it all might mean for the future of climate policy.

Holding our breaths until the election of our lifetimes

2026-10-15, updated: 2026-10-25

Donald Trump is accelerating his efforts at total control just prior to the crucial midterms. This IS, of course, the election of our lifetimes.

And the lifetime of America as a free democracy. If Democrats win back control of both houses from the do-nothing, enabling Republicans, the authoritarian madness can be stopped.

In the space of only the last few days, Trump’s minions have raided a Democratic Congressman’s house and have begun antitrust investigations of ALL the new outlets. Trump himself has made another deal with Putin that will allow Russia more funding to accelerate its assault on Ukraine, has now called into question the leadership of Ukraine, and spent a ten-minute rant in front of a crowd regarding how HE should have won the Nobel Peace Prize. His private army and police force (ICE) continues to terrorize American cities, still shooting innocents. And when I said ‘minions’, that is all that is left. The good people, the decent people have all said NO and either left or been fired. There exist no bulwarks any longer. Pete Hegseth, Todd Blanche, JD Vance, Tom Homan… continue the list and no one remains but minions, all in service of the most despicable human on the planet.

We’re in trouble. Unless the midterm results are a landslide, THEY will question the results. Mike Johnson (another minion) may refuse to seat and swear-in the newly elected majority.

And our greatest fear and expectation is that Trump is going to make up an excuse to call for a National Emergency prior to or at election time. We must hope those who also fear this will be ready, and that they’ll have judges on standby. Except for the U.S. Supreme Court, it has been the judiciary that has saved us so far by staving off issue after issue, even if it’s seemed to do so at glacial speed. Every American must vote November 3 and each must vote for America.

Vote for America. In the meantime, hold your breath.

Van Carter of Sioux Falls is a retired broadcast journalist and environmentalist who published a green website for 15 years.

via Sacramento Bee

The fall and (potential) rise of the South Dakota Democratic Party

2026-10-14, updated: 2026-10-25

Author’s note: The South Dakota Democratic Party has had a terrible 18 years since the loss of Tom Daschle and Stephanie Herseth Sanders and the eventual retirement of Tim Johnson. As of the general election of 2008, the South Dakota Democratic Party (SDDP)had 204,413 voters or 38.5% of registered voters, and the South Dakota Republican Party (SDRP) had 241.528 voters or 44.5% of the registered voters in South Dakota. By September 2026, the Democratic position had dropped by more than a third to 134,453 voters or 21.5% of registered voters while republicans increased by more than a third to 330,399 registered voters or 52.8%. Independent/No Party increased 87.6% from 83,147 to 156,019 registered voters or 25%.

The purpose of this article is to present a possible reason for the decline in SDDP registrations and propose ways of reversing it.

The Fall

No one knows for certain why voters chose not to register as Democrats and instead chose to register as IND/NPA or Republican. It is undoubtedly a variety of reasons. But what is clear is that beginning in 2009, the SDDP began to lose connection to and resonance with voters in South Dakota. In addition to the loss of voters, participation in the South Dakota legislature dropped from 34 members to nine. Nationally, our federal delegation dropped from three to zero. Several weaknesses have contributed to the decline:

Powerful and effective Opposition. The South Dakota Republican Party (SDRP) has been well organized, well funded and employed good strategy painting the SDDP as the party of high taxes, and minority groups.

Poor national perception The perception is not only attributable to the SDRP, the national Democratic Party’s lack of strategy has allowed this perception whereby the Republicans define us by issues rather than values.

Leadership. SDDP leadership selection is based on popularity only. No qualifications—knowledge, education experience, skills or abilities are required in order to lead the SDDP. This may be because of a lack of interested successful Democratic business and professional leaders. The SDRP, on the other hand has a large pool of business and professional leaders to call on to run their party and can select the one that they believe has the best skills to lead the party. Leadership will continue to be achallenge for the SDDP.

The Old Method of Growing the Party

Until recently, the SDDP had no real plan of action. Its efforts were focused on four areas:

Voter registration drives. The problem is that only one in five voters choose to register Democrat. The voter registration efforts were aimed at individually talking to potential voters and asking them to register as democrats. To the extent it occurred, it likely had positive effects and may have produced several thousand registered voters. At the same time thousands of registered democrats died or moved. And tens of thousands moved in with a net increase of nearly 100,000 voters. The personal contact technique is effective in registering a few voters, but not effective on a large scale.

To be successful, the first step in registering democratic voters is to convince them that the Democratic Party is the right choice. That requires “selling” the party to prospective voters BEFORE the second step of asking them to register.

Candidates. The second part of the existing plan is to get candidates that will grow the party. This is flawed, but based on experience. It has been candidates, not the leadership of the party that made it successful. Tom Daschle, and before him George McGovern, had the organization, management and marketing skills to develop a popular message and sell it to the public and create an organization to win voters and the election. However this is an unfair strategy and a losing one.

The party had its best, most popular, candidate in the last 15 years in Billie Sutton. Billie got approximately 50,000 independent and republican voters tovote for him. But they didn’t vote Democrat. Down ballot they voted Republican. And it wasn’t Bilie’s job to get people to vote Democrat. His only job was to get them to vote Sutton. It is the job of the SDDP to convince people to register and vote Democrat. They can’t require or expect candidates to do their job for them.

Support the Candidates. The party works with candidates to raise time and money, for their campaigns.

Get Out the Vote (GOTV). The party assists candidates in getting sympathetic voters out to vote. The problem is that if the marketing effort to create a solid base of sympathetic voters, there aren’t enough Democratic votes to get out to be successful.

All these activities are necessary. But they aren’t sufficient. Because they aren’t sufficient, the party has fallen on very hard times. The party needs to do more different things “work smarter”.

In recent years the party has developed some new ideas that form the basis of an informal plan. The success is yet to be determined. But there is reason to believe that the SDDP could rise to become more influential in South Dakota Public Policy.

The Rise

For the SDDP to rise again, several things must happen.

A solid plan that the SDDP adopts and follows the progress at every meeting — a process for selecting leaders that have the knowledge, skills, abilities and experience to successfully manage the party and implement the plan

The Plan

No large organization has been successful without a good plan. It has several names — Business Plan, Strategic Plan, Operations Plan, etc. — but a good plan has several items:

1. Values

These are the things that define the party. People with these values should be Democrats. They should be easily learned by everyone. Only two to five values with fewer than five words per value. Republicans have done an excellent job. Everyone knows the values that make a Republican. Republicans can differ on issues like data centers, pipelines etc., but on four critical areas they all have the same values. Even non- Republicans can easily define the values of a republican: Second amendment, right to life, small government, low taxes.

They are short. simple and easy to understand. They have other, hidden, values as well: rich people/money, white people, unrestricted business, etc. Those are not articulated, but reside in the background.

For Democrats, the definition is not so simple. The reason is that Democrats circle around issues, and republicans exploit that. They have been successful in defining a Democrat as a person that believes in (values) gays, trans, abortion, women, minorities, the “Green New Deal” etc. None of these are values. They are issues. Democrats need to define a short list of the values that define a democrat while they can disagree on specific issues. This is the “big tent” theory. The tent walls are the values anyone with those values is a Democrat. Issues are corners inside the tent. I suggest:

Value 1: People We value everyone, not just gays, trans, women, etc. But People. Anyone who values people should be a Democrat. That needs to be juxtaposed against the Republican value of money. If you think government should prioritize people over money, then you should be a Democrat. That idea needs to be sold.

Value 2: Good government We value government that is open, transparent, ethical and effective. Not necessarily cheap government—and that has been held against Democrats. But it should be efficient government.

Value 3. The environment. We value the world we live in. This would include everything from forest management to global warming. It could logically be included in good government or be stand alone.

I believe that most of the things that any Democrat values are subsumed in those values. Easy to define; easy to sell.

Vision: The vision is the outcome that the party is attempting to achieve. “The South Dakota Democratic Party envisions a state where…”

Mission. This is the primary reason for being and describes the method of making the vision come true.

Goals. A plan must have things it is working toward. Increased numbers of elected officials; improved funding; efficient administration are examples. As explained above, the party must market “sell” itself—its values. A strong marketing plan to reach all independents and “soft” republicans is necessary.

Objectives. These are measurable activities. They are certain things to be accomplished by an individual or group, by a certain date.

For a plan to be effective, it must be followed. Each quarterly SDDP agenda should include in addition to a consent agenda (reports, etc—things that need not discussion)

1. Old business:

a. What were we supposed to accomplish in the last quarter? What did we actually accomplish.

b. What were the successes and can be removed from the plan.

c. What were the failures and these added to new business.

2. New Business.

a. What things does the plan have us accomplish in the next quarter? Is that still realistic?

b. Should the plan be amended to include things left over?

3. Are there new issues that need to be added to the plan. Those apply to not for profit organizations as well as business organizations.

SUMMARY

The South Dakota Democratic Party must do two things in order to reverse the downward trend of the past two decades:

1. Develop a workable plan with goals and solid, measurable objectives. The plan must have clear values that define who is a Democrat. They must be as inclusive as possible. A small uniform party is comfortable, but ineffective. The party must believe in diversity for itself as well as for the nation. It cannot be a party of clones.

2. The party must develop a procedure for selecting leaders with a proven record of successful leadership of a large organization. “Learn on the job” is a recipe for failure, as our history shows. Learning from one’s mistakes is important. But it is best if those mistakes were made BEFORE becoming a SDDP leader. Learn at someone else’s expense, not ours.

John Cunningham of Sioux Falls has a Master of Public Administration degree. He has spent his career in local government finance, including in Fulton County, Ga., and Atlanta and has done consultant work in five foreign countries.

via NPR Economic

Wish we had an inter-tribal culture center in South Dakota

2026-10-13, updated: 2026-10-25

I took the pic above last weekend at the annual Black Hills Powwow in Rapid City, an event that had tribes from around the United States, Canada and Mexico participating. The small-framed image above doesn’t do justice to the breathtaking size and diversity of tribes that came together for this event.

Most inspiring to me is how these indigenous cultures were able to survive the rigors that “manifest destiny” inflicted on them during two centuries of westward expansion. The subjugation, displacement and cultural destruction that native peoples endured have been long-  and well-documented. The Black Hills Powwow is a showcase and testimonial to resilience and the bonds created by the compelling need for self-preservation.

As an Armenian whose family mostly survived the early 20th century holocaust and subsequent Christian genocide in Ottoman Turkey — my grandfather and namesake John the Baptist was put to death for the crime of being a Christian — I can relate to every drumbeat I heard at the Powwow.

I came away from the event wanting to know much more about the story of the Indians, particularly those of the Great Plains, who inhabited this land for many centuries before the European conquest of the Americas.

In my search for information and institutions that might supply narratives of the native inhabitants of the Great Plains I found that there isn’t a unique, comprehensive center where the different tribal histories of the region are housed.

We need a place that does just that. I wish that we had something here in South Dakota that’s similar to the Polynesian Cultural Center on Oahu in Hawai’i. The center calls itself “The vibrant cultures of 6 Pacific Islands in one unique place.” The cultures of six island nations are represented.

Between 700,000 and a million visitors see the Polynesian center annually. Given that millions of travelers pass through South Dakota just to see Mt. Rushmore and other historic sites every year, there’s a reasonable chance that a center devoted to a collective history of the various Indian tribes who’ve lived here for centuries would draw some interest and attract a respectable number of visitors.

The story of the indigenous cultures in the Great Plains is great and gripping. It needs to be showcased and easily accessible. Why the need? Because ultimately it’s the story of our selves. For good or bad, we were all in this together.

I’d sure love to see something like this materialize.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

via Sacramento Bee

Will Trump’s deal on Russian diesel lower fuel prices? It’s doubtful

2026-10-12, updated: 2026-10-25

In a last-ditch effort to get some price relief before the midterms, President Trump just struck a deal with Russia’s President Putin to provide 800,000 tons of Russian diesel fuel into American and global markets by the end of November and a few million more shortly thereafter.

Besides the trucking industry, American farmers also consume significant amounts of diesel fuel, which accounts for 44% of direct energy consumption on U.S. farms including, of course, those in South Dakota. You’d expect farmers to be cheered, but this transparently political turnaround from what has been longstanding policies against Russian fuel exports is a gimmick. I doubt that markets will see much of a drop.

Why not? mainly because The amount of diesel released by the Russians isn’t all that much. The first batch of diesel to be shipped out of Russia is 300,000 tons, which equates to about three-quarters of what the U.S. uses in a single day. The next batch released will be 500,000 tons by Novermber, soon followed by a 1 million ton release, then another 3 million tons “shortly after that.”

It sounds like a lot, but basically, we’re talking about a handful of days’ (maybe a couple of weeks) worth of supply.

Like, wowee.

We just went through this. Trump, as he did with his beef import scheme, comes up with what appears to be a big headline number to make it look like he’s doing something about inflation. Then we learn that the amount isn’t enough to make much of a difference in the market. Beef prices haven’t budged.

The same thing is likely to happen to diesel prices.

Yahoo Finance calls Trump’s initiative “The Art of the Tiny Deal” and says the amount promised will “do nothing” and that “this is not enough diesel to move the fuel gauge at all, much less lower diesel prices globally, or just the U.S. for that matter.”

More broadly, on a geo-political scale, Trump looks weak because he had to set aside sanctions against Russia that he signed just a month ago. The president is effectively saying that he didn’t mean to do that.

Trump’s history of position-shifting, of vacillation, goes on. It’s long-standing and it’s persistent. Politically, it’s his tragic flaw.

Meantime, Americans just keep paying up and paying up.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. I was leaving a parking lot when I saw a man jump out of his car, wave his arms, shake his fists and rant at a woman in a car that had nearly collided with his. Given the particulars of the near miss, it’s hard to say whose fault it would have been had they connected, but I can tell you whose side I would have taken. The guy was—and I mean no disrespect whatsoever when I say this—a bad-tempered, ill-mannered meathead. I rolled down my window and asked as gently as I could, “A little cranky, are we?”

No, I didn’t do that. Instead I decided to channel my dismay at the incident into educating grouches everywhere that the proper time for public displays of grumpiness is October 15th and only October 15th. That’s National Grouch Day, a day set aside to honor everyone’s favorite grouch, Oscar from “Sesame Street,” and to celebrate, or at least tolerate, all the grouches we know, possibly including…well…us.

If there’s a grump in your life, allow them to be as irritable as they want to be on October 15. Say nothing while they whine, complain and generally wallow in their misery all day long. But come October 16, tell them you and everyone else are sick and tired of it so they ought to just knock it off right now. That should cheer them up.

If it doesn’t—and it might not—try the following tips I found on that font of all wisdom, the internet.

  1. Gently explain to the grump that exercise causes our body’s natural pharmacy to release endorphins which are associated with feelings of happiness. Tell him he should take a long walk…off a short pier. Then say, “Haha! I’m joking! Isn’t it great? Laughter helps cure crabbiness too.”

  2. Give her a stick of gum. Apparently the repetitive action of chewing gum can be soothing. If that doesn’t do the trick, offer her a chew toy.

  3. Tell him doing something nice for someone else is a sure cure for crankiness. Then tell him what you’d like him to do for you.

  4. Give her chocolate. Eating chocolate makes some people happy. I’m one of them. So if she doesn’t care for chocolate, she should see rule number three and give hers to me. Then we’ll both be happy.

  5. Pets make people happy. Try giving the grouch a puppy.

  6. Decluttering has a calming effect, so tell the cranky person his house is a mess and he’d feel better if he’d just get himself organized. Who doesn’t love to hear good advice?

  7. Tell her to smile. The simple act of smiling can cheer us up. So the next time you encounter a crab, tell her as sweetly as you can to turn that frown upside down. It will either work or she’ll punch you.

  8. Tell him that rearranging furniture is a great day brightener. Changing an environment can help us feel refreshed. If he doesn’t want to move his furniture around, tell him he’s welcome to move yours.

  9. Play her some music. Music can turn a bad mood around. If there’s no music available, sing to the cranky person. If that doesn’t make her feel better, it may at least make her leave you alone.

  10. Encourage the crabby person in your life to count his blessings. Explain that if he keeps thinking about everything that’s wrong, his negative emotional state will continue. Certainly, he has much to be thankful for.  For one thing he’s got you to advise him.

Dorothy Rosby is an author and humor columnist whose work appears regularly in publications in the West and Midwest. You can subscribe to her blog at www.dorothyrosby.com or contact at www.dorothyrosby.com/contact .

via Sacramento Bee

Attorney urges care in choosing Secretary of State

2026-10-09, updated: 2026-10-25

Having practiced law for over 45 years, I can confirm that the Secretary of State is an office way too critical to be a political football. It’s a shame the election is even a partisan one.

The SOS protects the right to vote for every eligible voter and works with local officials to provide efficient, transparent, and fair elections. Thanks to state and local professionals and local volunteers, elections have never been a problem here. The SOS also handles campaign finance reports, registers lobbyists, processes ballot questions, commissions notaries, and delivers a host of other services to individuals and local governments.

The SD SOS also is critical to businesses and consumers in this state. SOS maintains information for all business entities operating in South Dakota and makes that information available online.

The office handles over 70,000 business filings each year, plus trademarks and Uniform Commercial Code filings important to lenders and property owners.

Dedication to competent, efficient, professional service is crucial.

Knowing all that, Republican incumbent Monae Johnson endorsed Terrence Davis. Despite the personal costs of endorsing a Democrat, Johnson explained that she could not remain silent because “the integrity, stability, and professionalism of this office is at stake.”

Likely, that’s because Republican candidate Heather Baxter is known as an election denier who neither respects the strength of our existing system nor understands the broad duties of the SOS.

Baxter ran for SOS only after coming in last in a primary election earlier this year for a legislative seat in her home district. Her focus is what she calls “election reform” – a euphemism for abandoning automation in favor of an inefficient, error-riddled plan of hand-counting all ballots.

Davis is a competent, reality-based professional who knows election administration is only one part of the job and knows it should not be politicized.

A former SD state trooper, Davis has a Master’s in public policy and experience in law enforcement and legal services, and is working on a doctorate in Law and Policy.

He respects the expertise of County Auditors, is committed to protecting voter information, and supports careful testing before implementing any major changes. Instead of retreating to pre-automation days, he advocates modernizing website services for businesses and consumers alike.

Terrence Davis, as Monae Johnson knows, is the best choice for SD Secretary of State.

Nancy Turbak Berry has practiced law in Watertown for 42 years. She has been a state senator, a state court magistrate judge, and an adjunct law professor.

via Market Place Tech Report

Why is Trump gutting a rural renewable energy program?

2026-10-08, updated: 2026-10-25

The USDA just issued a final ruling that will effectively end federal support for renewable energy projects on cropland. The program is The Rural Energy for America Program (REAP).

The decision is in keeping with President Trump’s long-standing hostility toward wind- and solar-energy projects. With regard to projects supported by REAP, the Trump administration, through Agriculture Secretary Brooke R. Rollins, calls them “unreliable” and adds that they “have not fully delivered on their stated goals.”

As to federal support,  Rollins says, “as of today that ends.”

South Dakota has participated in the program, to the tune of millions of dollars, in scattered parts of the state. USDA has touted the success of its projects in South Dakota, one of numerous states that have seen similar REAP-funded success stories.

Given that backdrop, the USDA decision to drop the program seems arbitrary and contrary to its history of success.

Indeed, EARTHJUSTICE, which describes itself as the nation’s “premier nonprofit public interest environmental law organization,” has filed a lawsuit against USDA, challenging its gutting of REAP.

Says EARTHJUSTICE: “ For decades, REAP had been a smashing success story. Since 2014, 19,000 farms and rural small businesses across all 50 states received REAP awards from USDA. According to USDA, in 2024 alone, the program awarded over $1 billion in REAP grants and loan guarantees nationwide , and generated or saved enough energy to power more than 300,000 homes . As late as May 2025, USDA touted REAP success stories , including the purchase of a 1.5 MW solar array by a farm in Habersham County, Georgia, which would “realize $176,490 per year of income and will generate 2,206 MWh per year, enough to power 204 homes.”

My take? I want to see some specificity from USDA as to how many REAP projects have been “unreliable” and “have not delivered as promised.” USDA itself boasts about the history of the program. Success stories in South Dakota and other states have had uniformly positive outcomes.

We need endeavors like REAP. Climate change is a fact. Says NASA, “there is unequivocal evidence that Earth is warming at an unprecedented rate. Human activity is the principal cause.”

Seems logical that the USDA should do all it can to facilitate the downshift of a man-made process that could do all of us in if we don’t change our ways.

via Market Place Morning Report

Trump tariffs are a work in progress … except there’s been no progress

2026-10-07, updated: 2026-10-25

Here’s yesterday’s headline from CNBC: “U.S. trade deficit hits $106.billion, widest since just before Trump tariffs enacted last year.”

That deflating news comes as no surprise.

Along with a ton of other people who have even a particle of knowledge on the subject, I’ve been pounding on Trump’s tariff policy since his first term. Basically, we skeptics argued that the president's tariff plan is bad for the economy and won’t do much good for our balance of trade.

Well, much as I hate to say ‘I told you so’ … I told you so.

August’s balance of trade numbers just came out, and at $106.5 billion, it's the widest gap since that jingoistic “liberation day” speech on April 2, 2025, which he said was “a date that  will forever be remembered as the day American industry was reborn, the day America's destiny was reclaimed, and the day that we began to Make America Wealthy Again."

Trump then held up a chart, later widely ridiculed, which he claimed was proof that “foreign leaders have stolen our jobs,  foreign cheaters have ransacked our factories, and foreign scavengers have torn apart  our once beautiful American dream.”

Looking for Trump-friendly support somewhere, anywhere, I find that supporters of the president’s trade policies are concentrated in a strongly conservative wing of the Republican party. Outside of that circle I can’t find much in the way of agreement with Trump, particularly among experts in the field.

Fact is, there isn’t much in the way of results that indicate Trump’s tariffs have done any good.

As to Trump’s rhetoric on “liberation day,” it  was not only head-shakingly hyperbolic, it was all wrong.

Trump’s tariffs have hurt, not helped, the American economy. AI sums it up: “These import taxes function as a direct financial burden that U.S. companies and families ultimately pay.”

Despite August’s leap to the upside, the overall 2026 trade deficit is lower than last year (by 20%) – an outcome which is to be expected after Trump’s tariff frenzy. As to positive gains for the economy,  mmm, the reduction has yet to bear any fruit. So far this year GDP growth is loping along at around 2%, about unchanged from 2025. As to inflation, this year’s rate of 3.37% is considerably higher than 2025’s 2.68%.

Researchers at the Federal Reserve Board last spring found that Trump’s tariffs have contributed nearly a percentage point to inflation, an outcome that was widely predicted by mainstream economists, including 16 Nobel laureates.

Trump ignored ample counsel and proceeded to turn his half-baked tariff scheme into a fully-baked tariff scam.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

via NPR Economic

What a less dominant America might mean for your money

2026-10-06, updated: 2026-10-25

I have long suggested owning companies outside the United States as part of a diversified investment portfolio. For most of that time it was unpopular advice. Americans did well betting on America, and the habit of holding primarily US stocks is deeply entrenched. Our brains are emotionally wired to buy what is familiar and hold what has increased in value.

American investors keep about 81% of their stock holdings at home, according to research from Vanguard, even though American companies make up roughly 60% of the world's stock markets.

A reason to look at that gap comes in a report by Phillips Payson O'Brien, titled " The American Age Is Over," published September 16, 2026, in The Atlantic. O'Brien, a professor of strategic studies at the University of St Andrews in Scotland, writes: "The American age that followed World War II was bound to end eventually. What's shocking is how suddenly that moment has arrived."

O'Brien builds part of his case on this year's war with Iran. In addition to the immediate costs of the war, stockpiles of the most advanced American munitions will take years to rebuild.

He also points out that longtime American partners are making their own arrangements, with Pakistan, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia signing a defense pact and South Korea warming to China. O'Brien sees this as part of a slower change that was already underway, writing, "The emergence of East Asia as the center of the world's economic output was always going to reduce American influence."

Both of these factors may affect your money. For example, China makes about 50% of the world's ships and controls about 80% of its drone manufacturing. The second and third largest shipbuilders are Japan and South Korea, while the United States does almost no civilian shipbuilding.

The other side of the case comes in a September 2, 2026, column in Directors & Boards, titled " The Shining City on a Hill," by Robert H. Rock. Rock grants that America has lost standing abroad, then writes: "Paradoxically, America's reputation abroad has weakened at the same time America's relative economic advantages have strengthened."

Only time will tell whether either O’Brien or Rock is right. In the meantime, it would not be helpful to overreact to either prediction. Neither fear nor unthinking confidence has much to do with the evidence.

What evidence does show is that a portfolio concentrated in one country does well only when that country does well into the future. The same thing is true of a nation's currency. If you earn dollars, spend dollars, and hold only dollar assets, you have taken a huge bet on the dollar, whether you intended to or not.

Let me emphasize that I am NOT suggesting the United States is finished or that you sell your American holdings. What I do suggest is that it would be worthwhile to consider what a less dominant America might mean for your money. Here are some suggestions: If you own index or target date funds, look at what is inside of them, because many hold American equities first, then international. Any additional  money you add could be diversified into international companies that earn in yen, euros, and pounds. If you are close to retirement, consider holding three years of living expenses in reserves to protect against needing to sell at the bottom of a market. Above all, make any changes gradually.

Diversifying your portfolio across the globe will not completely insulate you from a bad year in equities, because global markets tend to rise and fall together. However, that diversification can help shield your retirement resources from the decline of any single country.

Rounds' gas tax holiday? It's pandering. It's a terrible idea

2026-10-05, updated: 2026-10-25

Our Sen. Rounds just wrote a letter to the White House urging President Trump to suspend federal gasoline and diesel taxes through the end of the year. If you read the letter, you’ll see that Rounds is blaming a multitude of geo-political events, armed conflicts included, for the shortage of fuel that’s costing all of us plenty.

Rounds, like every other Republican running for office, is confronting an election season that sees GOP leader Trump in serious trouble with the electorate.The president’s approval ratings are dismal, so it comes as no surprise that Republican candidates are working overtime to find popular initiatives to curry some favor with voters. Rounds’ ploy is just another one of those rabbits coming out of a hat that is probably running low on schemes to bolster public support for the GOP.

This one is particularly obnoxious because its consequences are insidious and long term in nature. It sounds like a great, populist idea, just perfect for mesmerizing voters with its promise of cheaper fuel, but a gas tax holiday has costs that will result in serious longer term problems.

And not only that, it really doesn’t save you all that much money.

  • First off, as that doyenne of conservative thought, the Cato Institute, puts it, a gas tax holiday would be “expensive, ineffective and fiscally irresponsible.” Says Cato: “A three-month gas tax holiday would either accelerate the Highway Trust Fund’s insolvency by roughly nine months or require at least an $11 billion general-fund bailout. Meanwhile, the average driver would save only about $3 per fill-up.”

  • The Tax Policy Center, calling a federal gas tax holiday a “terrible idea,” makes the economic argument that a holiday would “increase consumption at a time of low supply, thus driving up pre-tax prices and worsening climate change.”

  • The Budget Lab calculates that a 3-month federal gas tax holiday would save the average household roughly $37. Whoopee.

  • The Tax Foundation headlines “Gas Tax Holidays Sound Politically Tempting. Too Bad They Don’t Work.” The Tax Foundation calls attention to the fact that “ pausing fuel taxes makes funding roads and highways more difficult while doing nothing to address the underlying issues driving prices upward.”

It’s tough to find supportive economic arguments for a gas tax holiday. In fact, I found it impossible. AI can steer you to a lot of verbiage about how it makes the government look like it’s doing something to help already cash-strained consumers. Trouble is, the argument overlooks the fact that the government’s economic and trade policies are responsible for making financial life tough for consumers in the first place.

Rounds won’t let up on his facile support for a gas tax holiday and of course will never acknowledge that people are financially strained because his party’s economic policies were fatally flawed from the get-go.

Will all this tax holiday talk do Republicans much good in November? I doubt it. The party’s rhetoric on inflation is transparently hopeless. Promoting a scheme like a gas tax holiday is another helping of GOP malarkey on the subject.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald.
